title: Attorney General of Oklahoma

context.text: Incumbent Attorney General Gentner Drummond ran for governor rather than seeking a second term, so the seat is open. Jon Echols won the June 16, 2026 Republican primary with nearly 55% of the vote over Jeff Starling; Nick Coffey was the only Democrat to file and his primary was canceled.

candidates.name: Jon Echols
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 16, 2026 Republican primary over Jeff Starling with nearly 55%.
candidates.currentRole: Attorney and business owner; Former Oklahoma House member (12 years)

summary.text: Jon Echols is the Republican nominee. He served in the Oklahoma House of Representatives for 12 years, eight of them as majority floor leader, and now practices law and owns businesses in Oklahoma City. He calls himself the "public safety candidate" and lists law-enforcement support, taxpayer oversight and prosecuting illegal marijuana grows among his priorities.

background.text: Undergraduate degree from the University of Oklahoma and law degree from Oklahoma City University.
Represented House District 90 for 12 years; named House majority floor leader after four years in office.
Co-founder of Shelter Oklahoma Schools, a charity that his campaign says has raised over $2.5 million for school storm shelters; has owned healthcare and construction companies.

priorities.text: Back law enforcement and defend liberties; defend taxpayers as a "watch dog" of tax dollars.
Defend private property rights, including protecting landowners from foreign adversaries, and maintain a working relationship with the state's sovereign tribal nations.
Ramp up prosecution of illegal marijuana grows with local law enforcement, enforce open records and open meetings laws, and work to settle the long-running poultry pollution lawsuit.

positions.summary: Lists protecting girls' sports from participation by "biological males" among his campaign priorities.
positions.quote: protect our daughters from biological males in women’s sports

statements.quote: As somebody who’s 100% pro-life, I would follow the law,
statements.context: On how he would handle a lawsuit challenging Oklahoma's abortion ban, as reported by Oklahoma Voice

record.text: Served in the Oklahoma House for 12 years, including as House majority floor leader (about eight years, per Oklahoma Voice).
His campaign says he created the Legislative Office of Fiscal Transparency (a campaign claim; not independently verified here).
Says he filed a bill to clarify the definition of "terminal" in state law and allow early induction of labor in terminal cases (his account to Oklahoma Voice; bill number not located).

candidates.name: Nick Coffey
candidates.ballotNote: Only Democrat to file; the Democratic primary was canceled.
candidates.currentRole: Federal prosecutor, Western District of Oklahoma (his campaign site uses the present tense; Oklahoma Voice calls him a former federal prosecutor)

summary.text: Nick Coffey is the Democratic nominee. A fifth-generation Oklahoman and graduate of the University of Oklahoma College of Law, he is a federal prosecutor (described by Oklahoma Voice as a former one) in the Western District of Oklahoma who has handled drug-trafficking, money-laundering and firearms cases. His priorities are rooting out public corruption, public safety, protecting children and watching taxpayer spending.

background.text: Federal prosecutor for the Western District of Oklahoma; served on the Department of Justice's Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Force.
Named Prosecutor of the Year by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Oklahoma in 2024, and by Homeland Security Investigations in 2023, according to his campaign.
Graduate of the University of Oklahoma College of Law.

priorities.text: Root out corruption in state government: "our elected Oklahomans should be held to a higher standard."
Crime: crack down on illegal firearms in the wrong hands, fight drug cartels and protect children from online predators.
Costs: watch tax dollars and expose business practices that take advantage of Oklahomans.

statements.quote: But right now, with what they’re describing, it is inhumane.
statements.context: On a lawsuit by women who say Oklahoma's abortion ban forced them to leave the state for care, as reported by Oklahoma Voice

researchNotes: Slate: the State Election Board's candidate list book (filing, April 2026) shows Echols and Starling (R) and Coffey (D); results were confirmed by Oklahoma Voice (June 16, 2026) and News 9 (Oct 13, 2026) and Ballotpedia. No independent or third-party candidate was found. Neither candidate holds this office; Echols's legislative votes were not reviewed bill by bill (the legislature's roll-call pages were not retrieved). Coffey's federal casework is described only through his campaign site. Echols's marijuana-farmland claim on his site was not verified. Oklahoma's Secretary of State is appointed by the governor, so there is no SoS race.
